title: Cesta domov
subtitle: The way home: a story in ten postcards

chapters.title: Prílet

beats.text: Your plane touches down in Bratislava. Through the glass doors you spot {partner}, grinning, holding a sign with your name on it.
He grabs your suitcase. "Test time," he says. "Read me the signs."

beats.prompt: He reads the big sign over the doors out loud. Which spelling did he say?

options.hint: Listen to the first vowel again. He held it long.
Close, but ô is a glide ("uo"). He said a plain o.

beats.text: In the taxi, the driver asks where to. {partner} hands you the address and leaves the talking to you.

beats.prompt: The driver repeats the street name. Which sign is it?

options.hint: Hissing or hushing? That first sound was "sh": š.
Right sound, wrong vowel: the long one is the u.

beats.text: At the hotel you pay. Time to thank the driver.

options.hint: So close. The first letter is the soft one: ď.

beats.text: {partner} squeezes your hand. "You read like a local already. Tomorrow: my parents."

chapters.postcard:
You made it. I'd imagined you walking through those doors so many times. Every Slovak sign you can read is one less thing between you and my world.
— J.

chapters.title: Zoznámenie

beats.text: The train pulls into {hometown}. {partner}'s parents are waiting at the door: Mama in her apron, Otec pretending he isn't nervous.

beats.prompt: Mama opens the door. How do you greet her?

options.hint: Sweet, but too casual for his mom. Use the formal greeting.
That's "good night", and it's three in the afternoon!
That's asking her name back (and informally). Answer first!
That's "I'm doing well". She asked your name.

reply.sk: Výborne! Lepšie ako ja po anglicky.

options.hint: Honest, but you understood him perfectly! Tell him you speak a little.

beats.text: A tiny woman with enormous energy bursts out of the kitchen and pinches your cheek.

beats.sk: Ty si tá Američanka! Aká pekná!

options.hint: That's "please / you're welcome". Thank her first.

chapters.postcard:
When you left the room, my mom leaned over and whispered: "Tá je zlatá." She's a gem. I told her I know.
— J.

chapters.title: Nedeľný obed

beats.text: Sunday. Babka has been cooking since six in the morning. The table could feed a small village.

options.hint: That's for drinks (and sneezes). For food: Dobrú chuť!
Wrong time of day. That's good night!
Probably true, but she asked if you like it!

beats.text: Your bowl is refilled before you can blink. Then comes the meat. Then the dumplings. Then more meat.

options.hint: Brave. You will regret it. Try declining politely.

beats.text: She puts more meat on your plate anyway. {partner} leans over: "Nobody has ever won against Babka."

options.hint: Understandable, but add "Prosím si", and remember káva → kávu.

beats.text: The whole table goes quiet. Any number will do; she'll tell the whole village either way.

reply.sk: Ešte mladá! A kedy bude svadba?
reply.en: Still young! So when's the wedding?

reply.sk: Ešte mladá! A kedy bude svadba?
reply.en: Still young! So when's the wedding?

beats.text: {partner} chokes on his Kofola.

chapters.postcard:
Babka asked about you three times on the phone this week. Not about me. About you.
— J.

chapters.title: Večer v meste

beats.text: One evening in Bratislava, just the two of you. The castle glows white above the Danube.

options.hint: Harsh! Try again.

beats.text: A tiny café in the old town. The waiter appears.

beats.en: Good evening, what will you have?

options.hint: Víno is neuter, so it doesn't change. Just víno.

beats.text: Later you need the restroom and can't see a sign anywhere.

reply.en: At the back, on the left.

options.hint: Prepáč is informal. With a stranger, use Prepáčte.
That asks the time!

beats.prompt: You'd like to pay by card.

options.hint: He already knows what it costs. Ask about the card.

beats.text: Walking up to the castle, the whole city sparkling below, {partner} stops and turns to you.

options.hint: Romantic moment, {name}! Food later.
Fair, it's chilly. But he's waiting for something else.

reply.sk: Teším sa na zajtra s tebou.
reply.en: I'm looking forward to tomorrow with you.

chapters.postcard:
I've walked past that castle a thousand times. It only became my favourite place in Bratislava when you were standing next to it.
— J.

chapters.title: Babkin recept

beats.text: Babka has decided you're ready for the family secret: bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep cheese.

beats.en: Today we cook together. What do we need?

beats.text: She points at the potatoes, the flour and a tub of bryndza (sheep cheese, feminine), and waits.

beats.prompt: Say "We need bryndza". Careful with the ending!

options.hint: It's the thing you need, so feminine -a becomes -u.
Not quite: -a → -u.

beats.en: Do you have brothers or sisters?

options.hint: A brother is a living masculine noun, so add -a: brata.

beats.en: And does Jakub help you at home?

beats.text: Behind Babka's back, {partner} is nodding frantically.

options.hint: Jakub is "he": robí, not robím.

beats.text: Babka hands you the grater. Forty minutes later you've made your first halušky. They're lumpy. Babka declares them perfect.

chapters.postcard:
Babka only teaches halušky to family. Draw your own conclusions.
— J.

chapters.title: Výlet do Tatier

beats.text: A weekend in the High Tatras. You're hiking up to a mountain hut above the clouds, and the last stretch is steep.

options.hint: That's "I have to". You mean "I can".

beats.text: At the hut: steaming tea, and a view over half of Slovakia. That evening, Mama calls on video.

options.hint: She asked where you WERE. Use the past tense.
After v, the place changes: v Tatrách.

reply.en: Beautiful! And what did you see?

beats.prompt: You saw a kamzík (a chamois, a mountain goat)! Say it as a woman.

options.hint: That's how a man says it. You're videla.
The -ý endings are for men. You're unavená, šťastná.

chapters.postcard:
Somewhere above the clouds you stopped asking me how to say things and just said them. I noticed.
— J.

chapters.title: Prvý deň v nemocnici

beats.text: A Bratislava hospital has invited you to visit its psychiatry department. The head physician, primár Horváth, meets you in the corridor.

beats.sk: Dobrý deň, pani doktorka. Vitajte u nás.

options.hint: That's the male form. You're a psychiatrička.

reply.en: Excellent. We have a patient for you.

beats.text: Pani Nováková, 45, sits in the consulting room, clutching her handbag.

options.hint: That's informal (ty). With patients, always vy.
You already know her name. Ask what brings her in.

reply.sk: Už mesiac sa cítim zle. Stále som smutná.
reply.en: I've felt bad for a month. I'm always sad.

options.hint: Ouch, that's "it's not a problem". Try empathy.
Informal, and too casual here.

beats.sk: Výborne, pani doktorka. Hovoríte ako slovenská lekárka.
beats.en: Excellent, doctor. You sound like a Slovak doctor.

chapters.postcard:
You walked into a Slovak hospital and asked the right questions, in Slovak. I told the whole family group chat. Mama replied with eleven heart emojis.
— J.

chapters.title: Konzultácia

beats.text: Week two. Pán Kováč, 60, has been referred by his GP for insomnia.

reply.sk: Zle. Budím sa o tretej ráno.
reply.en: Badly. I wake up at three in the morning.

options.hint: That's only about last night. Ask about his sleep in general.
That's "are you hungry right now?". Ask about appetite.

reply.sk: Nie veľmi. Schudol som päť kíl.
reply.en: Not really. I've lost five kilos.

beats.text: You need to ask about risk. You take a breath.

reply.en: No, not that. I have grandchildren.

options.hint: Important too, but ask about suicidal thoughts first.
Save that for the end.

beats.prompt: Explain the plan: one tablet a day.

reply.sk: Dobre. A kedy to začne účinkovať?
reply.en: OK. And when will it start working?

options.hint: Good advice, but first tell him how to take it.
Good line, but he asked when it starts working.

options.sk: Účinok nastúpi o dva až štyri týždne.

options.hint: Not with patients!

chapters.postcard:
Most people learn a language to order coffee. You learned one to sit with people on their worst days. That is the most you thing in the world.
— J.

chapters.title: Svadba: klebety

beats.text: Cousin Lucia's wedding. Three hundred guests, a live band, and Teta Zuzka, the family's chief gossip, has claimed the seat next to yours.

beats.sk: Počula si? Vraj je Lucia tehotná!
beats.en: Did you hear? Apparently Lucia's pregnant!

options.hint: She wants a reaction, not thanks!

beats.sk: A vidíš toho chlapa pri bare?
beats.en: And do you see that guy by the bar?

reply.sk: To je Luciin bývalý! Rozišli sa minulý rok.
reply.en: That's Lucia's ex! They broke up last year.

options.hint: That's "where is it?". You want "who".

beats.text: You start to turn around.

beats.sk: A tá v červených šatách je o dvadsať rokov mladšia ako jej manžel!
beats.en: And the one in the red dress is twenty years younger than her husband!

reply.sk: Áno, áno! Ale ja som ti nič nepovedala.
reply.en: Oh yes! But I didn't tell you anything.

options.hint: Wrong person, and wrong gender!

beats.text: Suddenly the woman in the red dress gets up and walks straight toward your table.

options.hint: Too late for that!

chapters.postcard:
Teta Zuzka told me you're "one of us" now. From her, that's the highest honour in the family. Also: everything she tells you is supposedly a secret.
— J.

chapters.title: Prípitok

beats.text: Midnight. The band stops. Lucia's veil is about to be swapped for a married woman's cap: the čepčenie. Otec appears with two little glasses.

beats.sk: Na zdravie! Pozri sa mi do očí!
beats.en: Cheers! Look me in the eyes!

options.hint: That's for food. For drinks: Na zdravie!

beats.text: The band starts a slow song. {partner} holds out his hand.

options.hint: Not of him, surely!

beats.text: Across the room, Babka watches the two of you and nudges Mama.

beats.sk: No a kedy bude vaša svadba?

beats.text: {partner} laughs and spins you around. You understood every single word tonight.

chapters.postcard:
The end. Or the beginning.
Ďakujem, že sa učíš môj jazyk. Thank you for learning my language. It means more than I know how to say, in either one.
— J.
